Getting Started with Microsoft Dynamics 365 Business Central: A Graduate’s Guide to ERP & Functional Consulting

A practical, process-first guide to understanding ERP, Business Central, business processes and functional consulting.

By Sunil Badiginchala · Microsoft Certified Trainer & Business Central Functional Consultant

The core idea: Understand the business → Understand the process → Understand Business Central → Practise → Share.

If you are new to ERP or Business Central, do not try to memorise every screen. Start by understanding how a business operates, how transactions move through a process, and what changes in the system when a transaction is posted.

Start withERP fundamentals · Business departments · End-to-end processes
Then learnBusiness Central navigation · Master data · Documents · Posting & configuration
Finally practiseSales-to-Cash · Purchase-to-Pay · Ledger entries · Real scenarios
This guide is forGraduates, ERP beginners, professionals and career changers exploring ERP and consulting.

1. First, What Is ERP?

ERP stands for Enterprise Resource Planning. In simple terms, an ERP system brings different business processes and information together in one connected environment.

Think about a typical organisation:

  • Sales deals with customers and orders.
  • Purchasing deals with vendors and purchases.
  • Warehouse manages inventory and shipments.
  • Finance manages accounting, receivables, payables and financial reporting.

These departments are not independent. A sales order can affect inventory; inventory movements can affect costs; an invoice can affect receivables and revenue; and a payment affects the financial position of the organisation.

Consultant lens: When you learn ERP, ask “What is the business trying to accomplish?” before asking “Which page do I open?”

2. What Is Microsoft Dynamics 365 Business Central?

Microsoft Dynamics 365 Business Central is a business management and ERP platform that helps organisations manage and connect their business processes.

It brings together areas such as Finance, Sales, Purchasing, Inventory, Projects, Warehouse and reporting/analysis.

The beginner mindset

The important thing is not to think of Business Central as simply a collection of screens. Think in processes, not screens.

A customer does not care that the system has a “Sales Order” page. They care whether the organisation can receive the order, fulfil it, invoice it, receive payment and report on the result.

3. Think in Processes, Not Screens

A strong Business Central professional understands the process behind the screens. The same principle applies whether you are learning Sales, Purchasing, Inventory, Finance, Projects or Warehouse.

Customer→Sales Order→Shipment→Invoice→Payment→Ledger Entries

Ask yourself: If I change one step in this process, which other departments or records could be affected?

4. Sales-to-Cash: A Simple End-to-End Example

Imagine a customer wants to purchase products from a company. A simple process can be described as:

Customer→Sales Order→Shipment→Invoice→Payment→Ledger Entries
  • Customer — Correct customer master data is needed.
  • Sales Order — Capture products, quantities, prices and other required information.
  • Shipment — Record what was fulfilled and delivered.
  • Invoice — Create the customer’s billing transaction.
  • Payment — Record the customer payment and apply it to the open entry.
  • Finance — Transactions create financial and operational records.

5. Real Business Central Walkthrough: From Customer to Ledgers

The screenshots below are from the Business Central environment supplied for this guide. They turn the process-first idea into something you can actually inspect. Use them as learning evidence: do not stop at the document page — follow the transaction into the entries.

5.1 Customer Card — Start with Master Data

Figure 1. Customer Card — Adatum Corporation. Observe the customer number, name, address/contact information and other customer setup.

Functional Consultant questions: Is the customer master data complete? What payment terms, posting groups, dimensions, credit controls or other setup does the business require?

5.2 Sales Order — Capture the Business Requirement

Figure 2. Sales Order — Adatum Corporation. The order captures the customer and transaction dates, status and lines used to fulfil the business request.

Functional Consultant questions: What is being sold? In what quantity? At what price? Which location is involved? What delivery expectations or approvals exist?

5.3 Posted Sales Invoice — The Transaction Has Been Posted

Figure 3. Posted Sales Invoice — Adatum Corporation. This is the historical document created after posting; it provides a starting point for tracing the transaction.
Do not stop here. The consultant question is: “What did posting create or change?”

5.4 Customer Ledger Entries — What Happened to Receivables?

Figure 4. Customer Ledger Entries. The invoice and payment entries show how the customer’s receivable is represented in the ledger.

Look for the relationship: invoice creates an open customer transaction; a payment can be applied against it. This is the bridge between the operational document and receivables.

5.5 Item Ledger Entries — What Happened to Inventory?

Figure 5. Item Ledger Entries. Purchase movements for items are visible here, illustrating how inventory transactions become item ledger records.
Consultant lens: Inventory is not just a quantity on a card. Transactions create entries that support inventory history, quantity tracking and costing analysis.

5.6 General Ledger Entries — What Happened Financially?

Figure 6. General Ledger Entries. G/L entries provide the accounting view of posted transactions and are a key part of tracing financial impact.

The learning habit: Take one posted transaction and trace it. Ask which document created the entries, which accounts were affected, and which dimensions or posting information carried through.

6. What Does a Business Central Functional Consultant Do?

A Functional Consultant is not simply someone who knows where every button is. The role involves understanding the business, understanding requirements and translating those requirements into an appropriate Business Central solution.

  • Understand business processes and requirements
  • Translate business needs into Business Central functionality
  • Configure standard Business Central capabilities
  • Identify gaps and potential extensions or integrations
  • Support testing and user acceptance
  • Support data migration
  • Train users
  • Work with developers and technical consultants
  • Communicate with business stakeholders
The question to develop as a habit: “What business problem are we trying to solve?” That should come before “Which field do I need to configure?”

8. Skills That Help You Start

  • Business Process Knowledge — Understand how Finance, Sales, Purchasing and Inventory work.
  • ERP Fundamentals — Understand how transactions flow through an organisation.
  • Business Central Knowledge — Gradually learn navigation, setup and configuration.
  • Consulting Skills — Communication, requirements gathering, analysis and problem solving.
  • Technology Awareness — Excel, Power BI, integrations and basic AL awareness can be useful.
  • Learning Mindset — Practise, document, ask questions and keep learning.

9. How Should a Beginner Start Learning Business Central?

StepFocusOutcome
01Understand ERPLearn how businesses operate.
02Understand Business ProcessesStart with Sales-to-Cash and Purchase-to-Pay.
03Learn Business Central BasicsNavigation, master data, customers, vendors, items, G/L accounts and documents.
04Build Functional DepthDimensions, posting, workflows and reporting.
05Understand ImplementationRequirements, configuration, testing and data migration.
06Practise & ShareDemos, blogs, videos, practical scenarios and community participation.

10. Don’t Just Learn the Screens — Understand What Happens When You Post

Don’t just learn what to click. Learn what happens after you click Post.

For a posted sales transaction, ask:

  • What happened to the customer?
  • What happened to receivables?
  • What happened to revenue?
  • What happened to VAT?
  • What happened to inventory?
  • What dimensions were posted?
  • Which ledger entries were created?

This way of thinking helps you move from simply using Business Central towards understanding Business Central.

11. Publishing Case Study: 500 Copies

Imagine we are implementing Business Central for a publishing organisation. A customer places an order for 500 copies of a new title.

Process stageConsultant question
CustomerIs the customer master data complete?
Sales OrderWhat information is required to capture the order?
InventoryAre 500 copies available?
ShipmentHow will the delivery be recorded?
InvoiceHow will the customer be invoiced?
FinanceWhat accounting and reporting impact will the transaction have?

The important lesson is that the consultant does not immediately start configuring fields. The consultant starts by asking questions and understanding the business process.

12. Business Central Across Different Industries

  • Publishing / Media — Products, sales, fulfilment, subscriptions, royalties and finance.
  • Retail — Customer sales, inventory, fulfilment, invoicing and payments.
  • Distribution — Inventory allocation, warehouse operations, picking, shipping and receivables.
  • Manufacturing — Planning, production, consumption, output, inventory costing and finance.
  • Professional Services — Projects, resources, time, expenses and project billing.
  • Projects / Construction — Planning, resources, item usage, costs, progress and billing.
The industry may change; the consultant approach stays consistent: Understand the business → understand the process → identify the requirement → design the solution.

13. You Don’t Need to Know Everything to Start

If you are a graduate or beginner, you may be thinking: “But I don't have Business Central experience.” That is okay.

Your existing knowledge can be a foundation. Finance, accounting, business, supply chain, IT, Excel, customer service, operations, project management and business analysis can all connect to ERP learning.

A better first goal: Become comfortable explaining one complete business process in Business Central.

Start with Sales-to-Cash. Once you can explain one process well, move to another.

14. Build Practical Experience — Not Just Certificates

Certifications can be valuable, but they should not be the only evidence of your learning. Create a demo environment and practise realistic transactions.

  1. Create a customer
  2. Create an item
  3. Create a sales order
  4. Ship the order
  5. Invoice it
  6. Look at the posted entries
  7. Understand the financial impact
  8. Explain the process to someone else

Then repeat the exercise with purchasing. Document what you learn through blogs, videos, demonstrations, community discussions and practical scenarios.

Portfolio idea: Build a collection of scenarios and solutions — not just certificates.

15. Try It Yourself: Your First End-to-End Exercise

Use a demo company and choose a simple product. Your objective is not speed; it is explanation.

  • A. Master Data — Create or identify a customer and item. Explain why each important field matters.
  • B. Transaction — Create a sales order. Record the quantity, price and any required operational information.
  • C. Posting — Post the transaction using the appropriate process for your scenario.
  • D. Trace the Document — Open the posted sales document and identify its document number and posting date.
  • E. Trace the Customer — Open Customer Ledger Entries and find the related transaction.
  • F. Trace Inventory — Open Item Ledger Entries and identify the relevant item movement.
  • G. Trace Finance — Open General Ledger Entries and identify the accounting impact.
  • H. Explain It — Explain the complete flow to another person without opening the system.

Questions to Answer After the Exercise

  • What business problem did the transaction solve?
  • Which master data records were involved?
  • Which document represented the operational transaction?
  • What changed after posting?
  • Which customer, item and G/L entries were created?
  • What would you investigate if the expected entries were not created?
  • Could you explain the process to a business user?

16. Your Journey Can Start Today

Explore ERP↓Learn Business Central↓Build Functional Knowledge↓Practise↓Share↓Grow as a Professional

You do not need to know where the entire journey ends. You need to know the next step.

Learn something. Practise it. Explain it. Share it. Then learn the next thing.

Final Thoughts

If you are considering a career in ERP or Microsoft Dynamics 365 Business Central, don't try to learn everything at once.

  • Start with the fundamentals.
  • Understand how businesses operate.
  • Learn the business process.
  • Then learn how Business Central supports that process.
  • Practise it.
  • Ask questions.
  • Share what you learn.

The goal is not just to know the software. It is to understand a business problem and help turn it into a practical solution.

“Understand the business. Understand the process. Understand Business Central. Then keep practising.”
